name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press
instructions: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, bar racked at the front of the shoulders.
Brace your core and glutes to keep the torso rigid.
Press the bar straight overhead until arms are fully extended.
Lower the bar back to the shoulders with control.
coachNote: Keep the ribcage down and glutes squeezed throughout — don't lean back to substitute for shoulder strength.
tips: Move your head slightly back as the bar passes your face, then push it forward under the bar at lockout.
Keep the bar path as vertical as possible.
commonMistakes: Excessive lower back arch to help drive the bar up.
Pressing the bar forward instead of straight up.
benefits: Builds full shoulder and core strength together.
One of the best raw indicators of upper-body pressing strength.
safetyNotes: Avoid pressing behind the neck if shoulder mobility is limited.
Use a spotter or squat rack safety pins for heavy attempts.
startingPosition: Bar racked at the front of the shoulders, elbows slightly forward.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead, bar above the crown of the head.

name: Seated Barbell Overhead Press
instructions: Sit on an upright bench with the bar racked at shoulder height.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Press the bar straight overhead until arms are fully extended.
Lower back to the shoulders with control.
coachNote: The seated position removes leg drive, isolating the shoulders and triceps more directly than the standing version.
tips: Keep your back flat against the bench pad.
Avoid arching excessively to compensate for a lack of shoulder strength.
commonMistakes: Bouncing the bar off the shoulders between reps.
Flaring the elbows out too wide at the bottom.
benefits: Removes lower-body momentum for stricter shoulder work.
Good progression tool once standing press technique is solid.
safetyNotes: Use a rack with adjustable safety pins.
Keep wrists stacked over the elbows.
startingPosition: Seated, bar racked at shoulder height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Push Press
instructions: Stand with the bar racked at the front of the shoulders, feet hip-width apart.
Dip slightly at the knees, then explosively drive up through the legs.
Use the leg drive momentum to press the bar overhead to full extension.
Lower the bar back to the shoulders with control.
coachNote: The leg dip should be short and fast — this is a power exercise, not a slow squat-and-press.
tips: Keep the torso upright during the dip, don't lean forward.
Time the press to start right as the legs finish driving.
commonMistakes: Dipping too deep, turning it into a push jerk.
Pressing before the legs finish their drive.
benefits: Allows heavier overhead loads than a strict press.
Builds explosive full-body power.
safetyNotes: Master the strict press before adding leg drive.
Use a rack or platform with adequate overhead clearance.
startingPosition: Bar racked at the shoulders, knees slightly bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead, legs extended.

name: Behind-the-Neck Press
instructions: Sit or stand with the bar racked behind the head at shoulder level.
Press the bar straight up until arms are fully extended.
Lower the bar with control back behind the neck.
coachNote: This requires above-average shoulder mobility — skip it if you feel any pinching or discomfort in the shoulder joint.
tips: Use a lighter load than a front press to start.
Keep the range of motion shallow if mobility is limited.
commonMistakes: Forcing excessive range of motion without adequate mobility.
Craning the neck forward to make room for the bar.
benefits: Can target the lateral delts slightly differently than a front press.
Useful accessory for lifters with good shoulder mobility.
safetyNotes: Stop immediately if you feel shoulder impingement.
Use light weight and a spotter when learning.
startingPosition: Bar racked behind the neck at shoulder height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Z Press
instructions: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight in front of you, bar racked at shoulder height.
Keeping the torso completely upright, press the bar overhead to full extension.
Lower back to the shoulders with control.
coachNote: Sitting on the floor removes any leg drive or leaning, forcing strict core-braced pressing strength.
tips: Sit as tall as possible before initiating the press.
Use lighter loads than a standing press — this is a strict strength builder.
commonMistakes: Leaning back to help drive the bar up.
Letting the legs bend to assist the movement.
benefits: Builds strict pressing strength and core stability together.
Exposes and corrects overhead pressing weaknesses.
safetyNotes: Start very light to learn the strict positioning.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Seated on the floor, legs extended, bar at shoulder height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead, torso upright.

name: Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press
instructions: Sit on an upright bench holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height.
Press both dumbbells overhead until arms are extended.
Lower with control back to shoulder height.
Repeat for the desired reps.
coachNote: The seated back support makes this an accessible, joint-friendly entry point into overhead pressing.
tips: Keep wrists stacked over the elbows.
Don't let the dumbbells drift too far forward or back.
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back excessively.
Flaring elbows too wide at the bottom.
benefits: Trains each shoulder independently, reducing imbalances.
Greater range of motion than a barbell press.
safetyNotes: Get dumbbells into position using your knees, not by swinging them up.
Use a weight you can control through the full range.
startingPosition: Dumbbells at shoulder height, elbows bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Standing Dumbbell Shoulder Press
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height.
Brace the core and press both dumbbells overhead.
Lower with control back to shoulder height.
coachNote: Standing adds a core-stability demand on top of the pressing work compared to the seated version.
tips: Avoid leaning back to drive the weight up.
Keep the ribcage down and core tight throughout.
commonMistakes: Using the legs to help push the dumbbells up.
Excessive lower back arch.
benefits: Builds shoulder strength alongside core stability.
No bench required, easy to set up anywhere.
safetyNotes: Start lighter than the seated version until balance is established.
Keep a stable, hip-width stance.
startingPosition: Standing, dumbbells at shoulder height.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Arnold Press
instructions: Sit holding dumbbells in front of the shoulders with palms facing you.
As you press up, rotate the palms to face forward at the top.
Reverse the rotation as you lower back to the starting position.
coachNote: The rotation adds extra time under tension through the full range of the deltoid, not just the pressing muscles.
tips: Keep the rotation smooth and continuous, not a separate step.
Control the descent through the same rotational path.
commonMistakes: Rushing the rotation and losing the extra tension benefit.
Using too much weight and turning it into a standard press.
benefits: Trains the deltoid through a fuller range of motion.
Combines pressing with a rotational stimulus for more complete development.
safetyNotes: Use a moderate weight to control the rotation properly.
Keep the movement smooth, not jerky.
startingPosition: Dumbbells in front of the shoulders, palms facing the body.
endingPosition: Arms extended overhead, palms facing forward.

name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Shoulder Press
instructions: Stand or sit holding a single dumbbell at shoulder height.
Press the dumbbell overhead to full extension while resisting torso rotation.
Lower with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Bracing the core against the offset load is just as valuable here as the shoulder work itself.
tips: Keep the hips and shoulders square, resisting the urge to lean.
Brace the free hand on your hip or a rack for extra stability if needed.
commonMistakes: Leaning excessively toward the working side.
Using momentum instead of controlled strength.
benefits: Corrects left-right shoulder strength imbalances.
Adds an anti-rotation core training benefit.
safetyNotes: Start with a lighter load than your bilateral press.
Keep footing stable throughout.
startingPosition: Dumbbell at shoulder height in one hand.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended overhead.

name: Machine Shoulder Press
instructions: Sit in the machine with back flat against the pad and handles at shoulder height.
Press the handles up until arms are extended.
Return with control back to shoulder height.
coachNote: A stable, guided option for beginners or for training close to failure safely without a spotter.
tips: Adjust seat height so handles align with shoulder level.
Avoid locking elbows out aggressively at the top.
commonMistakes: Seat set too high or low, changing the pressing angle unintentionally.
Using momentum by bouncing at the bottom.
benefits: Guided path reduces stabilizer demand.
Easy to progressively overload with the weight stack.
safetyNotes: Check seat position before loading heavy.
Keep wrists neutral throughout.
startingPosition: Handles at shoulder level, elbows bent.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Smith Machine Shoulder Press
instructions: Position a bench under the Smith machine bar and sit with the bar at shoulder height.
Unrack the bar and press it overhead until arms are extended.
Lower with control back to shoulder height.
coachNote: The fixed bar path allows safe training near failure without a spotter.
tips: Position the bench so the bar path lines up over the shoulders.
Keep the twisting motion controlled when racking.
commonMistakes: Bench misaligned with the bar path.
Forgetting to lock the bar before letting go.
benefits: Allows safe near-failure training.
Fixed path reduces stabilization demand.
safetyNotes: Confirm the safety hooks are set correctly.
Double check the bar is locked before releasing.
startingPosition: Bar racked at shoulder height, seated.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Landmine Shoulder Press
instructions: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment or corner.
Hold the loaded end at shoulder height with both hands.
Press the bar up and forward until arms are extended.
Return with control to shoulder height.
coachNote: The arcing bar path is easier on the shoulder joint than a straight overhead press, making it a good option for lifters with shoulder discomfort.
tips: Keep the core braced throughout the press.
Stand close enough to the pivot for a comfortable arc.
commonMistakes: Standing too far from the pivot, limiting range of motion.
Arching the back to help drive the bar up.
benefits: Joint-friendly pressing angle.
Easy to load and unload compared to dumbbells.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly in the landmine attachment.
Start light to learn the bar path.
startingPosition: Bar held at shoulder height with both hands.
endingPosition: Arms extended forward and upward.

name: Single-Arm Landmine Press
instructions: Hold the loaded end of a landmine barbell at shoulder height with one hand.
Press the bar up and forward until the arm is extended.
Return with control, then complete reps before switching sides.
coachNote: Bracing against the single-arm load builds anti-rotation core strength alongside the shoulder work.
tips: Brace the core to resist rotating toward the working side.
Drive through the legs slightly for stability.
commonMistakes: Letting the torso twist excessively.
Standing too close to the pivot point, limiting range.
benefits: Joint-friendly angle for pressing.
Trains core stability alongside the shoulders.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly.
Start light to learn the bar path.
startingPosition: Bar held at shoulder height, standing in a staggered stance.
endingPosition: Arm extended forward and slightly upward.

name: Kettlebell Overhead Press
instructions: Clean or lift a kettlebell into the rack position at shoulder height.
Press the kettlebell overhead until the arm is fully extended.
Lower with control back to the rack position.
coachNote: The kettlebell's offset center of mass demands more stabilization than a dumbbell of the same weight.
tips: Keep the wrist neutral, not bent back, throughout the press.
Brace the core to avoid leaning to the side.
commonMistakes: Letting the kettlebell roll onto the wrist during the press.
Excessive side bend to compensate for the offset load.
benefits: Builds shoulder stability alongside strength.
Transfers well to other kettlebell and functional training movements.
safetyNotes: Learn the rack position with a lighter kettlebell first.
Keep footing stable throughout the press.
startingPosition: Kettlebell in the rack position at shoulder height.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended overhead.

name: Bottoms-Up Kettlebell Press
instructions: Hold the kettlebell upside down by the handle, bell facing the ceiling.
Press it overhead while keeping the bell balanced and stable.
Lower with control back to shoulder height without losing the balance.
coachNote: This is primarily a grip and shoulder-stability drill — use very light loads and expect a slow, deliberate tempo.
tips: Grip the handle firmly with a vice-like hold.
Move slowly and stay focused on keeping the bell vertical.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight, causing the bell to tip over.
Rushing the tempo instead of controlling every inch.
benefits: Builds exceptional shoulder and grip stability.
Improves overhead control that carries over to heavier pressing.
safetyNotes: Start with a very light kettlebell.
Practice near a soft surface in case the bell tips.
startingPosition: Kettlebell held upside down at shoulder height.
endingPosition: Arm fully extended overhead, bell balanced.

name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Raise both arms out to the sides until roughly shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: This is the classic side-delt builder — prioritize a light-to-moderate weight with a strict path over ego lifting.
tips: Lead with the elbows, not the hands.
Keep a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the dumbbells up.
Raising the arms above shoulder height, which shifts tension to the traps.
benefits: Directly builds shoulder width via the side delts.
Simple, equipment-light isolation move.
safetyNotes: Avoid using a weight so heavy it forces momentum.
Keep the shoulders down, away from the ears.
startingPosition: Dumbbells at the sides, slight elbow bend.
endingPosition: Arms raised out to the sides at shoulder height.

name: Seated Dumbbell Lateral Raise
instructions: Sit upright on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Raise both arms out to the sides until roughly shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The seated position removes the ability to use body momentum, keeping the tension strictly on the side delts.
tips: Sit tall throughout the set.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
commonMistakes: Leaning to one side to help lift the weight.
Using too much weight and losing the strict form.
benefits: Removes momentum for a stricter isolation.
Good option when a bench is available for extra stability.
safetyNotes: Keep a light-to-moderate weight to protect the shoulder joint.
Avoid raising above shoulder height.
startingPosition: Seated, dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Arms raised out to the sides at shoulder height.

name: Cable Lateral Raise
instructions: Stand sideways to a low cable pulley, gripping the handle with the far hand.
Raise the arm out to the side until roughly shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cables keep constant tension on the side delt throughout the range, unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the bottom.
tips: Keep a slight forward lean away from the machine for a fuller stretch.
Lead with the elbow throughout the raise.
commonMistakes: Using the whole body to swing the handle up.
Standing too close to the machine, limiting the stretch.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the full range of motion.
Easy to adjust angle by changing pulley height.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Avoid raising above shoulder height.
startingPosition: Arm across the body at the low pulley, handle in hand.
endingPosition: Arm raised out to the side at shoulder height.

name: Leaning Cable Lateral Raise
instructions: Hold onto the cable machine frame with the free hand and lean away from it.
Raise the working arm out to the side until roughly shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Leaning away from the machine puts the side delt under tension right from the very bottom of the rep, unlike a standard standing lateral raise.
tips: Lean from the hips, not the whole body swinging.
Keep the raise slow and controlled.
commonMistakes: Standing too upright, losing the bottom-range tension benefit.
Using momentum to jerk the handle up.
benefits: Increases tension at the bottom of the movement.
Strong hypertrophy stimulus for the side delts.
safetyNotes: Hold the frame securely while leaning.
Use a lighter weight than a standard lateral raise to start.
startingPosition: Leaning away from the machine, arm across the body.
endingPosition: Arm raised out to the side at shoulder height.

name: Machine Lateral Raise
instructions: Sit in the machine with arms against the pads, elbows near your sides.
Raise your arms out to the sides until roughly shoulder height.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A great beginner-friendly isolation move since the machine controls the movement path for you.
tips: Adjust seat height so the pivot aligns with the shoulder joint.
Focus on a slow, controlled tempo rather than heavy loads.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight and shrugging the shoulders up.
Rushing through reps with momentum.
benefits: Very beginner-friendly with a fixed, safe path.
Good side-delt isolation without stabilizer demand.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat and pad position correctly before loading.
Avoid raising above shoulder height.
startingPosition: Arms against pads at the sides.
endingPosition: Arms raised out to the sides at shoulder height.

name: Lu Raise
instructions: Stand holding light dumbbells at your sides.
Raise the arms out and slightly up in an arc, rotating the thumbs toward the ceiling at the top.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The upward arc and end rotation shifts more emphasis onto the often-underdeveloped upper portion of the side delt.
tips: Use lighter weight than a standard lateral raise — the extended range makes this harder than it looks.
Keep the movement smooth through the full arc.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight and cutting the arc short.
Rushing the top rotation.
benefits: Targets the upper side delt fibers more than a standard raise.
Adds variety to combat side-delt training plateaus.
safetyNotes: Start very light to learn the pattern.
Avoid shoulder impingement by keeping the motion controlled.
startingPosition: Dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Arms raised out and up, thumbs rotated toward the ceiling.

name: Resistance Band Lateral Raise
instructions: Stand on the middle of a resistance band, holding one end in each hand at your sides.
Raise both arms out to the sides until roughly shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient, joint-friendly option for travel or home shoulder training when dumbbells aren't available.
tips: Stand wider on the band for more resistance.
Keep a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
commonMistakes: Using a band too heavy to control with strict form.
Shrugging the shoulders during the raise.
benefits: Portable and joint-friendly.
Constant tension throughout the range of motion.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
startingPosition: Standing on the band, hands at the sides.
endingPosition: Arms raised out to the sides at shoulder height.

name: Dumbbell Front Raise
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs.
Raise one or both arms straight out in front of you to shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The front delts already get significant work from pressing movements — treat this as a light accessory, not a primary builder.
tips: Keep a slight bend in the elbows throughout.
Avoid swinging the weight up using the hips.
commonMistakes: Using momentum from the lower back to heave the weight up.
Raising above shoulder height.
benefits: Direct isolation for the front delts.
Simple to perform with minimal equipment.
safetyNotes: Use light-to-moderate weight since front delts fatigue quickly from pressing work.
Keep the core braced to avoid arching the back.
startingPosition: Dumbbells in front of the thighs.
endingPosition: Arms raised to shoulder height in front of the body.

name: Barbell Front Raise
instructions: Stand holding a barbell in front of your thighs with an overhand grip.
Raise the bar straight up to shoulder height, keeping arms mostly straight.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Using a bar fixes both hands together, which can make it harder to cheat the weight up compared to dumbbells.
tips: Keep the bar close to the body as it rises.
Avoid leaning back to generate momentum.
commonMistakes: Using the lower back to swing the bar up.
Raising the bar too high above shoulder level.
benefits: Simple front-delt isolation movement.
Fixed grip width keeps both arms symmetrical.
safetyNotes: Use a light load — this is not a heavy-load exercise.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Bar held in front of the thighs.
endingPosition: Bar raised to shoulder height.

name: Plate Front Raise
instructions: Hold a weight plate with both hands in front of your thighs.
Raise the plate straight up to shoulder height, keeping arms mostly straight.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The plate's grip demand adds a forearm and grip component on top of the front delt isolation.
tips: Grip the plate at the edges for a secure hold.
Keep the raise slow and controlled.
commonMistakes: Using momentum to swing the plate up.
Gripping the plate too loosely, causing instability.
benefits: Adds a grip-strength component to a front raise.
Simple, minimal equipment needed.
safetyNotes: Use a plate weight you can control comfortably.
Keep the core braced to protect the lower back.
startingPosition: Plate held at the thighs with both hands.
endingPosition: Plate raised to shoulder height.

name: Cable Front Raise
instructions: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley holding the handle in one hand.
Raise the arm straight up in front of you to shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cables keep constant tension on the front delt throughout the range, unlike a dumbbell which loses tension at the bottom.
tips: Keep the working arm mostly straight throughout.
Avoid using the torso to help lift the handle.
commonMistakes: Leaning back to add momentum.
Raising the arm above shoulder height.
benefits: Constant tension through the full range of motion.
Easy to adjust load in small increments.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a light-to-moderate weight.
startingPosition: Arm down at the low pulley, handle in hand.
endingPosition: Arm raised to shoulder height in front of the body.

name: Resistance Band Front Raise
instructions: Stand on the middle of a resistance band, holding one end in each hand at your thighs.
Raise both arms straight up to shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A convenient front-delt option for home or travel training when no dumbbells or cables are available.
tips: Stand wider on the band to increase resistance.
Keep the movement slow and controlled.
commonMistakes: Using a band too heavy to control with strict form.
Raising above shoulder height.
benefits: Portable, minimal equipment needed.
Adjustable resistance via stance width.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Keep the core braced throughout.
startingPosition: Standing on the band, hands at the thighs.
endingPosition: Arms raised to shoulder height.

name: Barbell Upright Row
instructions: Stand holding a barbell in front of your thighs with a shoulder-width grip.
Pull the bar straight up toward your chin, leading with the elbows.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Stop pulling once the elbows reach shoulder height — going higher increases shoulder impingement risk for many lifters.
tips: Keep the bar close to the body throughout the pull.
Lead with the elbows, not the hands.
commonMistakes: Pulling the bar too high, straining the shoulder joint.
Using a grip too narrow, which increases impingement risk.
benefits: Builds the side delts and traps together.
Good compound accessory for shoulder development.
safetyNotes: Use a wider grip if you feel shoulder discomfort.
Stop the pull at shoulder height.
startingPosition: Bar held at the thighs.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up to roughly chest/collarbone height, elbows high.

name: Cable Upright Row
instructions: Stand facing a low cable pulley holding a straight bar attachment.
Pull the bar straight up toward your chin, leading with the elbows.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Cable tension stays constant throughout, which many lifters find more comfortable on the shoulder than a barbell version.
tips: Keep the bar close to the body.
Stop the pull at shoulder height.
commonMistakes: Pulling too high and straining the shoulder.
Using body momentum to move the weight.
benefits: Constant tension throughout the range.
Easy to fine-tune the load.
safetyNotes: Use a wider grip if shoulder discomfort occurs.
Keep the movement controlled.
startingPosition: Arms extended down, holding the bar attachment.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up toward the chin, elbows high.

name: Dumbbell Upright Row
instructions: Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs.
Pull both dumbbells straight up toward your chin, leading with the elbows.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Dumbbells allow a slightly more natural hand path than a fixed barbell, which some lifters find more comfortable.
tips: Keep the dumbbells close to the body.
Stop the pull at shoulder height.
commonMistakes: Pulling too high, causing shoulder strain.
Using momentum instead of a controlled pull.
benefits: Slightly more natural wrist path than a barbell.
Builds side delts and traps together.
safetyNotes: Stop the pull at shoulder height.
Use a moderate weight to maintain control.
startingPosition: Dumbbells held at the thighs.
endingPosition: Dumbbells pulled up to roughly chin height, elbows high.

name: Wide-Grip EZ Bar Upright Row
instructions: Stand holding an EZ bar with a wide grip in front of your thighs.
Pull the bar straight up toward your chest, leading with the elbows.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The angled EZ bar grip combined with a wider hand spacing tends to be more comfortable on the wrists and shoulders than a straight bar.
tips: Use a grip noticeably wider than shoulder-width.
Keep the pull height at or below shoulder level.
commonMistakes: Using a narrow grip, which increases shoulder strain.
Pulling too high.
benefits: More wrist-friendly than a straight barbell.
Effective side delt and trap builder.
safetyNotes: Keep the pull height controlled.
Use a moderate weight to maintain strict form.
startingPosition: EZ bar held at the thighs with a wide grip.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up toward the chest, elbows high.

name: Dumbbell Scaption Raise
instructions: Stand holding a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Raise the arms out at roughly a 30-degree angle in front of the body (between a front and lateral raise) to shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The scapular plane angle is often more shoulder-friendly than a strict front or lateral raise, making this a good option for lifters with shoulder sensitivity.
tips: Keep thumbs pointed slightly upward throughout.
Use a light weight to prioritize the correct angle.
commonMistakes: Drifting into a strict front or lateral raise path.
Using too much weight and losing the angle.
benefits: Shoulder-friendly raise angle.
Trains the delts through a natural movement plane.
safetyNotes: Keep the load light.
Stop at shoulder height.
startingPosition: Dumbbells at the sides.
endingPosition: Arms raised at a 30-degree angle to shoulder height.

name: Cable Y-Raise
instructions: Stand facing away from a low dual-cable pulley holding a handle in each hand.
Raise both arms up and out into a 'Y' shape overhead.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: This trains the lower traps and shoulder stabilizers that are often neglected in standard pressing and raise work.
tips: Use light weight and focus on the exact Y-shaped path.
Keep the shoulder blades depressed throughout.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight and shrugging up.
Turning it into a standard front raise instead of the Y angle.
benefits: Strengthens often-neglected scapular stabilizers.
Complements pressing and raise work for balanced shoulder health.
safetyNotes: Keep the load very light — this is a technique-focused exercise.
Move slowly through the full range.
startingPosition: Arms down and together in front of the body.
endingPosition: Arms raised overhead in a Y shape.

name: Cuban Press
instructions: Perform an upright row with dumbbells until elbows reach shoulder height.
From that position, rotate the forearms up so the dumbbells point toward the ceiling.
Press the dumbbells overhead, then reverse the entire sequence to return to the start.
coachNote: This combines three movements in one rep, making it a great shoulder health and stability exercise, not just a hypertrophy tool.
tips: Use very light dumbbells — this is a technical exercise.
Move slowly through each of the three phases.
commonMistakes: Rushing through the rotation phase.
Using weight too heavy to control the rotation properly.
benefits: Trains the rotator cuff and scapular stabilizers alongside the delts.
Improves overhead pressing mechanics.
safetyNotes: Start with very light weight to learn the sequence.
Stop if any shoulder pinching occurs.
startingPosition: Dumbbells at the thighs.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead after the rotation.

name: Cable External Rotation
instructions: Stand sideways to a low cable pulley with the elbow bent 90 degrees and tucked to your side.
Rotate the forearm outward and away from the body, keeping the elbow fixed.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A key rotator cuff exercise for shoulder health — keep the elbow pinned to your side throughout the entire movement.
tips: Use a very light weight — this is a health and stability exercise, not a strength builder.
Keep the elbow tucked and stationary.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow drift away from the body.
Using too much weight, recruiting the larger shoulder muscles instead.
benefits: Strengthens the rotator cuff.
Helps balance out internally-rotated pressing-dominant training.
safetyNotes: Keep the load light.
Stop if you feel any joint discomfort.
startingPosition: Elbow bent 90 degrees, forearm across the body.
endingPosition: Forearm rotated outward, away from the body.

name: Cable Internal Rotation
instructions: Stand sideways to a low cable pulley with the elbow bent 90 degrees, forearm out to the side.
Rotate the forearm inward across the body, keeping the elbow fixed.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: Pair this with external rotations to build balanced rotator cuff strength on both sides of the joint.
tips: Keep the elbow pinned to the side throughout.
Use a light, controlled weight.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow drift forward or away from the body.
Using momentum instead of a controlled rotation.
benefits: Balances rotator cuff strength alongside external rotation work.
Supports shoulder joint health long-term.
safetyNotes: Keep the load light.
Stop if any discomfort occurs.
startingPosition: Elbow bent 90 degrees, forearm out to the side.
endingPosition: Forearm rotated inward across the body.

name: Side-Lying Dumbbell External Rotation
instructions: Lie on your side holding a light dumbbell in the top hand, elbow bent 90 degrees and tucked to your ribs.
Rotate the forearm upward, keeping the elbow fixed against the body.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: A staple rehab and prehab exercise for the rotator cuff — very light weight is intentional here.
tips: Keep the elbow glued to your side throughout.
Move slowly through the full range.
commonMistakes: Letting the elbow lift away from the ribs.
Using a weight too heavy for strict rotator cuff isolation.
benefits: Strengthens the rotator cuff in a stable, supported position.
Common in shoulder injury prevention and rehab programs.
safetyNotes: Use a very light dumbbell.
Stop immediately if any pinching occurs.
startingPosition: Lying on the side, elbow bent 90 degrees, forearm against the stomach.
endingPosition: Forearm rotated upward, elbow still tucked to the ribs.

name: Band Pull-Apart
instructions: Hold a light resistance band with both hands, arms extended in front of you at shoulder height.
Pull the band apart by driving the hands out to the sides, squeezing the shoulder blades together.
Return with control to the starting position.
coachNote: A simple, effective warm-up staple before any pressing or overhead work.
tips: Keep the arms at shoulder height throughout.
Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end range.
commonMistakes: Bending the elbows to make the pull easier.
Using a band too heavy to control smoothly.
benefits: Improves shoulder posture and health.
Quick, equipment-light warm-up option.
safetyNotes: Check the band for wear before use.
Keep the movement smooth and controlled.
startingPosition: Arms extended forward at shoulder height, holding the band.
endingPosition: Arms extended out to the sides, band stretched across the chest.

name: Pike Push-Up
instructions: Start in a downward-dog position with hips raised and hands on the floor.
Bend the elbows to lower the top of your head toward the floor.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: A great bodyweight progression toward a handstand push-up — increase the hip angle over time for more overhead-style loading.
tips: Keep the hips high throughout the movement.
Look slightly forward, not straight down, to protect the neck.
commonMistakes: Letting the hips drop, turning it into a regular push-up.
Going too fast without control.
benefits: No equipment needed.
Builds pressing strength that transfers toward handstand push-ups.
safetyNotes: Build regular push-up strength first.
Progress the range of motion gradually.
startingPosition: Downward-dog position, hips high, hands on the floor.
endingPosition: Top of the head near the floor, elbows bent.

name: Elevated Pike Push-Up
instructions: Place your feet on an elevated surface such as a bench, hands on the floor, in a pike position.
Bend the elbows to lower the top of your head toward the floor.
Press back up to the starting position.
coachNote: Elevating the feet increases the overhead-pressing angle, moving this closer to a true handstand push-up.
tips: Keep the hips high and body in a pike shape throughout.
Progress the bench height gradually.
commonMistakes: Feet elevated too high before building enough strength.
Losing the pike position under fatigue.
benefits: Increases difficulty without added weight.
Strong progression step toward a handstand push-up.
safetyNotes: Choose a stable elevated surface.
Master the standard pike push-up first.
startingPosition: Feet elevated, hands on the floor, hips high.
endingPosition: Top of the head near the floor.

name: Wall-Supported Handstand Push-Up
instructions: Kick up into a handstand against a wall for support, hands shoulder-width apart.
Lower your head toward the floor by bending the elbows.
Press back up to the starting handstand position.
coachNote: This is an advanced bodyweight pressing movement — build up through pike push-up progressions first.
tips: Keep the core braced and body in a tight line against the wall.
Use a folded mat or pad to cushion the head at the bottom.
commonMistakes: Flaring the elbows out wide.
Attempting this before mastering elevated pike push-ups.
benefits: Builds exceptional overhead pressing strength.
High-level bodyweight shoulder and triceps development.
safetyNotes: Practice near a wall with a spotter if possible.
Use a soft surface for the head to touch down on.
startingPosition: Handstand position against a wall, arms extended.
endingPosition: Head lowered near the floor, elbows bent.

name: Deficit Handstand Push-Up
instructions: Set up a handstand against a wall with hands placed on elevated blocks or plates.
Lower your head down into the gap below hand level.
Press back up to the starting handstand position.
coachNote: Only attempt this once standard handstand push-ups are comfortable for multiple reps — the deficit significantly increases the demand.
tips: Use stable, secure elevation blocks.
Keep the core tight throughout the extended range.
commonMistakes: Using an unstable or uneven elevation setup.
Progressing to a deficit before mastering the standard version.
benefits: Increases range of motion for greater strength development.
Advanced progression for elite pressing strength.
safetyNotes: Ensure the elevation surfaces are completely stable.
Have a spotter present when learning.
startingPosition: Handstand position, hands elevated on blocks.
endingPosition: Head lowered into the gap below hand level.

name: Wall Handstand Hold
instructions: Kick up into a handstand against a wall for support.
Hold the position with arms extended and core braced.
Lower down with control once the hold is complete.
coachNote: A foundational hold for building the shoulder stability and confidence needed before attempting handstand push-ups.
tips: Press firmly through the hands to keep the shoulders active.
Keep the core braced to avoid an excessive back arch.
commonMistakes: Letting the lower back sag into an arch.
Holding the breath instead of breathing steadily.
benefits: Builds shoulder and core stability under load.
No equipment needed beyond a wall.
safetyNotes: Practice near a clear, padded area.
Have a spotter when learning to kick up.
startingPosition: Handstand position against a wall.
endingPosition: Same handstand position held statically.

name: Iso-Lateral Shoulder Press Machine
instructions: Sit in the machine gripping the independent handles at shoulder height.
Press the handles up until arms are extended, one or both sides at a time.
Return with control to shoulder height.
coachNote: The independent handles let each arm move through its own natural path, useful for correcting side-to-side imbalances.
tips: Keep the back flat against the pad.
Press evenly if working both arms together, or focus on strict form if training one side at a time.
commonMistakes: Letting the stronger side dominate the rep.
Using excessive weight and shortening range of motion.
benefits: Allows unilateral or bilateral training on the same machine.
Guided path reduces stabilizer demand.
safetyNotes: Adjust seat height correctly before loading.
Keep wrists neutral throughout.
startingPosition: Handles at shoulder height, seated.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Smith Machine Upright Row
instructions: Stand with the Smith machine bar set at thigh height, gripping it shoulder-width.
Unrack the bar and pull it straight up toward your chin, leading with the elbows.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The fixed bar path removes any forward-backward drift, keeping the pull strictly vertical.
tips: Keep the bar close to the body throughout.
Stop the pull at shoulder height.
commonMistakes: Pulling too high and straining the shoulder.
Using too much weight and losing strict form.
benefits: Fixed path reduces stabilization demand.
Easy to control the range of motion precisely.
safetyNotes: Use a wider grip if shoulder discomfort occurs.
Confirm the bar is unlocked before pulling.
startingPosition: Bar racked at thigh height.
endingPosition: Bar pulled up toward the chin, elbows high.

name: Resistance Band Overhead Press
instructions: Stand on the middle of a resistance band, holding a handle in each hand at shoulder height.
Press both hands straight overhead until arms are extended.
Lower with control back to shoulder height.
coachNote: A useful travel or home option when no dumbbells or barbell are available — band tension increases as you press higher.
tips: Stand wider on the band to increase resistance.
Keep the core braced throughout the press.
commonMistakes: Leaning back to help drive the band up.
Using a band too heavy to control at the top of the range.
benefits: Portable, minimal equipment needed.
Adjustable resistance via stance width or band tension.
safetyNotes: Inspect the band for wear before use.
Ensure secure footing on the band.
startingPosition: Handles at shoulder height, band under tension.
endingPosition: Arms extended overhead.

name: Viking Press (Landmine)
instructions: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment with a neutral-grip handle or V-bar over the loaded end.
Hold the handle at chest height with both hands, palms facing each other.
Press the bar straight up overhead until arms are extended.
Lower with control back to chest height.
coachNote: The neutral grip and arcing path make this one of the most shoulder-friendly heavy pressing variations available.
tips: Keep the core braced throughout the press.
Stand centered under the bar path for balanced pressing.
commonMistakes: Leaning back excessively to drive the weight up.
Standing off-center, causing uneven bar movement.
benefits: Shoulder-friendly angle allows heavier pressing loads.
Neutral grip reduces wrist and elbow strain.
safetyNotes: Secure the barbell end firmly in the landmine attachment.
Start light to learn the pressing path.
startingPosition: Handle held at chest height with both hands.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.

name: Bradford Press
instructions: Stand holding a barbell racked in front of the shoulders.
Press the bar partway up and forward, bringing it just past the top of the head.
Lower the bar behind the head to shoulder height without locking out overhead, then press back to the front.
Continue alternating front-to-back presses without ever reaching full lockout.
coachNote: Because the bar never locks out overhead, this keeps constant tension on the shoulders throughout the entire set.
tips: Use a light weight since the range of motion is unconventional.
Keep the movement slow and controlled throughout.
commonMistakes: Attempting a full range of motion overhead like a normal press.
Using too much weight, which limits the necessary control.
benefits: Removes any rest at lockout, maximizing time under tension.
Unique variation for breaking through shoulder training plateaus.
safetyNotes: Requires good shoulder mobility — skip if you feel any pinching.
Use light weight to prioritize safe technique.
startingPosition: Bar racked in front of the shoulders.
endingPosition: Bar alternated between front and back shoulder height without full lockout.

name: Egyptian Lateral Raise (Cable)
instructions: Stand sideways to a low cable pulley, leaning your torso away from the machine while holding onto a fixed support with the free hand.
Raise the working arm out to the side until roughly shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: The exaggerated lean shifts the resistance curve to make the bottom portion of the raise significantly more challenging.
tips: Lean as far as balance safely allows for maximum stretch.
Keep the movement slow and deliberate.
commonMistakes: Not leaning far enough to get the intended benefit.
Using a weight too heavy to control the lean.
benefits: Increases resistance at the bottom of the raise for greater stimulus.
Advanced variation for experienced lifters seeking new stimulus.
safetyNotes: Ensure a secure, stable hold on the support structure.
Use lighter weight than a standard cable lateral raise.
startingPosition: Leaning away from the machine, arm across the body.
endingPosition: Arm raised out to the side at shoulder height.

name: Single-Arm Cable Front Raise
instructions: Stand facing away from a low cable pulley set behind you, holding the handle in one hand.
Raise the arm straight up in front of the body to shoulder height.
Lower with control back to the starting position.
coachNote: Training one arm at a time allows a fuller focus on the mind-muscle connection with the front delt.
tips: Keep the working arm mostly straight throughout.
Avoid using the torso to help lift the handle.
commonMistakes: Leaning back to add momentum.
Raising the arm above shoulder height.
benefits: Addresses left-right strength imbalances.
Constant tension throughout the range of motion.
safetyNotes: Keep a stable, braced stance.
Use a light-to-moderate weight.
startingPosition: Arm down behind the body, handle in hand.
endingPosition: Arm raised to shoulder height in front of the body.

name: Kettlebell Halo
instructions: Hold a kettlebell by the horns at chest height.
Circle the kettlebell around your head, staying close to the skull, in one direction.
Complete the circle and repeat, alternating direction each set.
coachNote: An excellent shoulder mobility and warm-up drill before overhead pressing sessions.
tips: Keep the core braced to avoid excessive arching as the bell passes behind the head.
Move slowly and with control around the entire circle.
commonMistakes: Using a kettlebell too heavy to control smoothly around the head.
Rushing through the circle instead of a controlled pace.
benefits: Improves shoulder mobility and control.
Quick, effective warm-up for pressing days.
safetyNotes: Use a light kettlebell.
Keep the movement close to the head without hitting it.
startingPosition: Kettlebell held at chest height by the horns.
endingPosition: Kettlebell returned to chest height after a full circle around the head.

name: Reverse Grip Barbell Press (Bottoms-Up Press)
instructions: Stand or sit holding a barbell at shoulder height with an underhand (supinated) grip.
Press the bar straight overhead until arms are fully extended.
Lower the bar back to shoulder height with control.
coachNote: The underhand grip shifts more emphasis onto the front delts and can feel more shoulder-friendly for some lifters than a standard overhand press.
tips: Keep the elbows tucked slightly more than a standard press.
Use a lighter load than your standard overhead press to start.
commonMistakes: Using too much weight before adapting to the unfamiliar grip.
Flaring the elbows out wide.
benefits: Shifts emphasis toward the front delts.
Offers a shoulder-friendly grip alternative for some lifters.
safetyNotes: Start light to adapt to the grip.
Use a spotter or rack safety pins.
startingPosition: Bar held at shoulder height with an underhand grip.
endingPosition: Arms fully extended overhead.
